newsitem.title: USA: As stock falls, lawsuits allege Columbia/HCA misdeeds.
newsitem.headline: As stock falls, lawsuits allege Columbia/HCA misdeeds.

text.p: Shareholder lawsuits filed against officials of Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. rose in number to 11 this week as Wall Street pressured the stock on news of indictments in a massive federal investigation.
Three midlevel executives of the largest U.S. for-profit hospital firm, based in Nashville, Tenn., were indicted Wednesday on charges of fraud in an alleged billing scam.
Unnamed federal officials were quoted in news reports Thursday as saying that more indictments could come.

The shareholder lawsuits seek damages on behalf of investors who allege they have been harmed by numerous questionable business practices at Columbia that led to the crisis now confronting the Nashville, Tenn.-based firm.

"Essentially all the cases raise the same exact issues," said Joseph Lapofsky, an attorney at Zwerling Schachter & Zwerling, a New York law firm that filed one of nine cases pending in U.S. District Court in Nashville.

Those nine cases, filed between April and last week, along with two others filed in Chancery Court in Delaware in recent days, allege that Columbia followed some practices that, Lapofsky said, were "either illegal or bordered on fraudulent." They include:

-- Providing physicians with equity interests in Columbia hospitals or providing them with loans, consultation fees, below-market rents, vacations or other incentives in exchange for referrals of patients to Columbia hospitals;
-- Overbilling the federal Medicare programme by "upcoding" certain medical procedures, or making them seem more costly and thereby getting higher Medicare reimbursement payments;

-- Overbilling private insurers "using the same method of fraudulently overstating the injuries and medical conditions of their insured," according to the complaint filed in the case that Lapofsky is handling;
-- Following unfair labour practices in connection with a nurses' union drive at a Kentucky hospital; and
-- Selectively steering patients to home health care services financially affiliated with Columbia.
The lawsuits also allege that officers and directors of the company profited unfairly by trading in Columbia stock while in possession of material, non-public information.
Asked Tuesday to comment on allegations contained in the lawsuits, Columbia's new chief executive, Dr. Thomas Frist, told Reuters he has "zero tolerance" for any misconduct.

Frist was appointed Friday to replace Richard Scott as chairman and chief executive. "If I find, as a matter of fact, that there's anything unethical, the government isn't going to have to ask me to correct that," Frist said in an interview.
He said the company has halted and may unwind certain physician hospital syndication deals.
He declined to comment on the other allegations, saying he needed more time to find out the facts.

The value of Columbia stock has fallen sharply from more than 40 to the low 30s since mid-July, when a federal probe of the firm widened to six states and 33 facilities, prompting the resignation of Scott and President David Vandewater.
Columbia stock fell $1.6875 to $32.125 Thursday afternoon in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange as the market reacted to the indictments.
Alxe. Brown health care analyst Peter Emch called the charges "incrementally negative news" and downgraded his rating of Columbia to "market performer" from "buy."

Wheat First Butcher Singer health care analyst Joel Ray said ending the investigation probably means that Columbia will have to make a costly settlement with the government or face its ultimate regulatory sanction.
"They can threaten to take them out of the Medicare programme. That's the situation Columbia faces," Ray said.
Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements accounted for about 41 percent of Columbia's $19.9 billion in 1996 revenues.
Many health care providers have been excluded from the Medicare programme for breaking its rules.

But larger entities that run into trouble are more typically required to adopt and pay for a corporate integrity programme that is monitored by the government for a number of years, said a government spokesman.
